standard.title: Select grammar to enhance meaning
standard.description: select and use structures and features of the target language grammatical and writing systems to enhance meaning and create spoken, written and multimodal texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have developed knowledge of and can use key grammatical structures and writing system features of the target language — including agreement, verb conjugation, sentence construction and orthographic conventions (AC9LS8EU02). They have not yet selected and used more complex grammatical structures (comparatives, multiple tenses, complex sentences) to enhance meaning purposefully.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students select and use a range of grammatical structures — including comparatives, multiple tense forms, pronoun systems, cohesive devices and complex sentence constructions — to enhance meaning in spoken, written and multimodal target language texts.

nodes.label: Articles, agreement and determiner refinement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply article and agreement rules with increased accuracy, including in cases where the target language differs from expected patterns.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply definite and indefinite article rules correctly in at least five phrases, including at least one case that involves an exception or nuance from the basic rule.
nodes.typical_width: Use articles, possessives and demonstratives with accurate gender and number agreement; handle common exceptions and nuanced cases (e.g. omission rules, collective nouns, irregular patterns); apply agreement across complex noun phrases.
wider: Investigate how article use in the target language differs from English across specific contexts — create a reference guide for cases that are consistently challenging
Analyse a native speaker text for article usage — identify patterns that go beyond the rules taught and hypothesise about the additional conventions

response_modes.reason: Agreement accuracy is a fluency issue at Y9-10 — students typically understand rules but apply them inconsistently in production. Focused practice with nuanced cases and self-correction in drafting builds reliable application.

success_criteria: Applies article and agreement rules correctly in complex noun phrases including at least one exception or nuanced case
Self-corrects agreement errors during drafting when reviewing own work

nodes.label: Comparatives, superlatives and intensifiers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use comparatives and superlatives — including irregular forms — and intensifiers to express and nuance comparisons in the target language.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least three comparative or superlative forms correctly in a target language text.
nodes.typical_width: Use regular and common irregular comparative and superlative forms; use intensifiers to strengthen or weaken statements; apply comparison structures in informative and opinion texts.
wider: Compare how comparison is expressed across the target language and English — identify structural differences and cases where direct translation fails
Use comparatives and superlatives in a persuasive or review text — reflect on how comparison language shapes argument and evaluation

response_modes.reason: Comparative structures need to be practised across varied comparison contexts (people, places, ideas, options) to ensure transfer beyond one rehearsed topic area.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparative structures are directly needed for the opinion, discussion and evaluation tasks in EC01–EC02. Building comparative grammar fluency here directly enables richer participation in the communicating strand.
success_criteria: Uses at least three comparative or superlative forms correctly including at least one irregular form
Applies comparison structures in a text where comparison is genuinely purposeful (not just a grammar drill)

nodes.label: Tense variety and temporal expression
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and use multiple tense forms in the target language — including past tenses and immediate or simple future — to express temporal relationships.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least two different tense forms correctly in a single target language text (e.g. present and past, or past and future).
nodes.typical_width: Use present, past and future tenses in spoken and written texts; distinguish between different past tense forms where the target language requires this; use tense variation to sequence events and express temporal relationships.
wider: Compare how past tense forms in the target language differ from English past tense — identify what distinctions the target language makes that English does not require
Produce a narrative or personal account that uses at least three tense forms — reflect on how tense choice shapes the narrative perspective
nodes.hinge_reason: Tense variety is required for the extended text production demanded in EC06 and the reflection tasks in EC03. Students who are restricted to present tense cannot produce the narrative, reflective or informative texts the Y9-10 descriptors require. This also underpins EU03's metalinguistic analysis of tense systems.

response_modes.reason: Tense accuracy in production requires practice — students often understand tense concepts but apply them inconsistently when juggling other production demands. Narrative and reflective texts that require tense variation provide the practice context.
Tense forms need to be encountered and used across varied text types (narrative, reporting, planning, reflecting) to become flexible tools rather than practised paradigms.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Investigating how the target language's tense system encodes distinctions that English does not (or vice versa) is a rich metalinguistic and intercultural insight — different tense systems reflect different ways of conceptualising time and event.
success_criteria: Uses at least two different tense forms correctly in a single text
Can explain the distinction between at least two tense forms in the target language

nodes.label: Complex sentence construction and cohesive devices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct complex sentences and use cohesive devices in the target language to connect and develop ideas across a text.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce at least three complex sentences in a target language text using cohesive devices to connect ideas.
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of cohesive devices to connect and develop ideas; construct sentences with subordinate clauses, relative pronouns and prepositional phrases; use impersonal expressions and discourse markers to add nuance and manage text flow.
wider: Analyse the cohesive structure of a native speaker text — identify all cohesive devices and discuss their effect on the text's coherence and flow
Compare complex sentence construction in the target language and English — identify where the target language requires different syntactic choices for the same meaning

response_modes.reason: Complex sentence construction integrates the grammar and vocabulary knowledge from nodes 1–3 into extended, coherent text production. The move from producing individual sentences to constructing cohesive texts is the key integration challenge — tasks requiring multi-paragraph texts with explicit cohesive marking support this.

success_criteria: Produces a text with at least three complex sentences using cohesive devices to connect ideas
Uses at least two different cohesive devices correctly in the same text
